What still needs testing

I would not yet call the application fully tested. We still need more extensive randomized simulations, fixed-pair and voluntary sit-out scenarios, late arrivals and departures, Zoned Play regression testing, persistence/reloading, and real mobile-device interaction testing.

There's also a design issue worth correcting: G3 currently records games and social encounters when a round is generated, not when it is completed. That can distort fairness history if an organizer creates a round that never gets played.

I recommend resolving that before production deployment.

My assessment: G3.2.1 is ready for a controlled beta where you can experiment without depending on it for a live session. I would hold off on replacing your dependable Armory version until we've completed the remaining tests and addressed the round-history issue.

These are results from individual simulated sessions, not averages. The tests also covered 6, 10, and 24 players.

Every tested round had complete doubles games, no duplicate player assignments, and no observed JavaScript errors.

One particularly encouraging result: With 18 players using four courts, everyone encountered all 17 other players within 12 rounds, while receiving 10–11 different partners.

That is exactly the kind of social mixing we're aiming for.

Dynamic-participation tests

I also ran browser tests involving actual player registration, fixed pairs, voluntary sit-outs, and late arrivals.

The application successfully generated valid rounds after adding players, changing available courts, and adding a fixed pair. When one member of a fixed pair volunteered to sit out, both were marked to sit out together. The next round also handled two additional late arrivals without duplicate assignments or JavaScript errors.

These tests are encouraging, but they exposed an important limitation in the test setup: the application starts with four courts enabled, so my initial court-change sequence did not accurately represent the intended three courts → four courts → three courts progression. I'll correct that rather than count the mislabeled sequence as a passed test.

Corrected dynamic test: passed

The corrected test now confirms the exact scenario you described:

18 players · 3 courts

12 playing · 6 sitting

12 playing · 6 sitting

All three transitions generated valid court assignments.

What I still consider unresolved

I don't want to overstate the testing. We have good evidence that the basic scheduling works, but three areas deserve further attention:

  1. Round history: The code records games when the next round is generated, even if that round is subsequently canceled. This can affect fairness and social statistics.

  2. Social optimization: The results are promising, but we haven't completed a statistically meaningful head-to-head comparison against the previous G3 scheduler.

  3. Full regression coverage: Zoned Play, persistence after browser reload, unusual pairing combinations, and physical mobile-device testing remain incomplete.

I have not modified the G3.2.1 file during this testing.

My recommendation: You can upload G3.2.1 to a separate beta site for controlled experimentation, but I would not yet replace the version used for actual Armory sessions.

Before calling G3.2 production-ready, I'd address the round-history issue and complete the remaining regression tests. Those are more important than adding any further cosmetic features right now.
